abstract.p: The poem frames Sir Thomas Smith’s death through an extended prison metaphor. It imagines the grave as a place of temporary confinement, where the body remains imprisoned in its “stony Vault” until it has paid the final “fees” owed to “deaths greedy gaylours,” the worms of bodily corruption. Against this physical captivity, however, the poem sets the spiritual liberation of the soul: though the deceased had stood guilty of sin, he has been redeemed and cleansed by Christ’s blood, and his soul is therefore expected to attain a fuller freedom beyond the tomb.

div.head: Mr St: Clive: On Sir Thomas Smith

lg.l: As prisoners quite quit to gaine new libertie
Must fee their keepers or still captive lie
So this brave Knight (by his redeemers bloud
Cleansed from the Sinne where of he guilty stoode
Must in this stony Vault imprisoned stay
Till hee the Wormes (deaths greedy gaylours) pay
Theire uttmost fees: which by his Corpes discharg’d,
Ist like his freer soule shall bee ynlarg’d

div.head: Historical context and dating
div.p: This short funerary poem most likely commemorates Sir Thomas Smythe [Smith] (c. 1558–1625), the merchant and colonial administrator. He died on 4 September 1625 and was buried at Sutton-at-Hone, Kent, where he was commemorated by a substantial tomb, circumstances that fit the poem’s sepulchral setting and its image of confinement in a ‘stony Vault’. The poem should therefore date from shortly after his death, plausibly in late 1625 or the following years. Its identification is further supported by the existence of other contemporary elegiac verses on Sir Thomas Smith/Smythe, including William Strachey’s elegy on Sir Thomas Smith, knight (), and Joshua Sylvester’s poem ‘To the right vertuous ... Sir Thomas Smith (of London), knight’ ().
